title: The potential of naturally stress‐tolerant corals to enhance reef recovery and restoration—A systematic review of transplantation studies from marginal and extreme reefs
content:
Sourcing corals from marginal or extreme environments does not inherently enhance restoration success. Since resilience traits are context specific and may be neutral or detrimental outside their native conditions, effective coral transplantation requires careful environmental matching between donor and recipient sites, appropriate species and morphology selection, alongside long-term monitoring to ensure sustained outcomes.


Abstract

Corals persisting in marginal and extreme environments including turbid, mesophotic, high-latitude, mangrove and thermally variable reefs are hypothesized to possess stress-tolerant traits that could support reef recovery. Transplanting corals from these environments has therefore emerged as a potential reef restoration strategy. However, whether resilience traits are retained following relocation remains unclear. We conducted a systematic review and structured data synthesis of 306 coral transplantation measurements to assess whether corals sourced from marginal or extreme environments exhibited enhanced growth, survival or physiological performance in recipient habitats. Transplantation consistently elicited measurable biological responses, but outcomes were highly context dependent. Corals originating from mesophotic reefs showed uniformly positive growth responses at recipient sites, whereas survival responses were predominantly neutral (52.3%), with positive (26%) and negative (21.7%) outcomes occurring less frequently. Corals sourced from turbid reefs frequently exhibited enhanced growth following transplantation (71.4%), but their survival responses were mixed, with positive and negative responses occurring at similar frequencies, indicating that coral growth and survival responses can be decoupled across biological functions. Coral morphology significantly influenced results: branching corals were highly responsive to transplantation but exhibited variable (positive and negative) directional effects, whereas massive corals showed more moderate responses. Importantly, studies assessing coral transplantation for longer than 1 year demonstrated that early positive responses did not reliably predict long-term survival. Synthesis and applications: Sourcing corals from marginal or extreme environments does not inherently enhance restoration success. Since resilience traits are context specific and may be neutral or detrimental outside their native conditions, effective coral transplantation requires careful environmental matching between donor and recipient sites, appropriate species and morphology selection, alongside long-term monitoring to ensure sustained outcomes.
